11.0.big: Sexual reproduction mixes DNA from two parents. To do that, each parent makes special cells with only half the chromosomes, and two of them fuse into one new, unique cell.
points: Some organisms (yeast, sponges) can just clone themselves. Most multicellular life uses two parents.
Each parent makes a haploid cell, and fertilization joins two of them into a diploid cell with a brand-new mix of genes.
Some species can do both. Aging termite queens clone new queens (parthenogenesis).

11.1.big: Meiosis is one round of DNA copying followed by two divisions. It turns one diploid cell into four haploid cells, each genetically unique.
points: Meiosis I separates homologous pairs, cutting the chromosome sets from 2 to 1. That's why it's called the reduction division.
Prophase I: homologs pair up tightly (synapsis, held by the synaptonemal complex) to form tetrads. They swap pieces (crossing over) at chiasmata, which is variation source #1.
Metaphase I: pairs line up in random orientation (independent assortment), which is variation source #2. With 23 pairs, that's over 8 million (223) combinations.
Anaphase I: homologs separate, but the sister chromatids stay together.
Meiosis II works like mitosis: sister chromatids separate. There's no DNA copying beforehand (interkinesis has no S phase).
Mitosis makes 2 identical diploid cells. Meiosis makes 4 different haploid cells.
11.1.tip: Meiosis I splits the pairs (homologs). Meiosis II splits the sisters (chromatids), just like mitosis.

11.2.big: Sex is costly, but it makes varied offspring, and variety helps populations survive changing environments, predators and parasites.
points: Asexual reproduction is quick and needs no mate, but its only source of variation is mutation.
Sexual reproduction reshuffles genes three ways: crossing over, independent assortment, and random fertilization.
Red Queen hypothesis: species are always co-evolving with rivals and parasites, so they have to keep changing just to keep up.
Diploid-dominant (most animals, including you): the only haploid cells are gametes.
Haploid-dominant (fungi, some algae): the main body is haploid. The diploid zygote immediately does meiosis to make spores.
Alternation of generations (plants): a multicellular haploid gametophyte alternates with a multicellular diploid sporophyte.

2.why: The synaptonemal complex is the protein zipper that holds homologous chromosomes together as a tetrad.

3.why: Sister chromatids separate in anaphase II. Anaphase I separates homologous pairs.

4.why: By metaphase I the synaptonemal complex is gone, and homologs are held together only at the chiasmata (crossover points).

5.why: Interkinesis has no S phase: DNA isn't copied again before meiosis II.

6.why: Meiosis II separates sister chromatids, just like mitosis.

7.why: Spindle fibers aren't part of crossing over. That happens between paired homologs in prophase I, helped by recombination nodules.

8.why: The second source of variation is random alignment of homologous pairs in metaphase I.

9.why: Alternation of generations (plants) has both a multicellular haploid and a multicellular diploid stage.

10.why: In asexual reproduction, the only new variation comes from mutations in DNA.

11.why: Sex creates variation, which helps a population adapt and survive change.

12.why: In most sexual species, only half the population (the females) can bear offspring, so it grows more slowly than an all-female asexual population would.

13.why: Fungi are haploid-dominant: their main body is haploid.

14.why: In diploid-dominant organisms like animals, meiosis makes gametes (egg and sperm).

15.why: Tetrads form in prophase I of meiosis, line up at the metaphase plate, and each pair orients randomly, independently of the others.

16.why: Metaphase I lines up homologous pairs. Metaphase II lines up single chromosomes, each made of two sister chromatids.

17.why: Meiosis halves the chromosome number and adds variation. Mitosis does neither.

18.why: Each pair lines up randomly, so which parent's chromosome ends up in each gamete is random, and that creates new combinations.

19.why: As one species improves, its competitors have to improve too just to keep up, like running to stay in the same place.

20.why: Crossing over, random assortment and random fertilization all mix genes differently each time.

21.why: Diploid-dominant: humans. Haploid-dominant: fungi. Alternation of generations (both stages multicellular): plants.

22.why: Body cells are somatic cells. They're diploid, with double the chromosome number of gametes.

23.why: Spores are haploid reproductive cells that grow into haploid organisms by mitosis, with no fertilization needed.

24.why: The synaptonemal complex is a protein lattice that zips homologous chromosomes together along their whole length.

25.why: Crossing over happens between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during prophase I.

26.why: All three are random: where crossovers happen, how pairs line up, and which sperm meets which egg.

27.why: In diploid-dominant life cycles (animals), the only haploid cells are single-celled gametes.

28.why: The diploid sporophyte makes spores by meiosis.

29.why: (+) and (−) mating types belong to haploid-dominant life cycles like fungi. Both cycles have meiosis, spores and free-living haploid stages.
